papers.title: Tau positron emission tomography imaging in progressive supranuclear palsy: A review of phenotypes, symptoms, and clinical severity.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is an atypical parkinsonian four tandem-repeat (4R) tauopathy, predominantly affecting subcortical and brainstem regions, with later cortical involvement. PSP is frequently misdiagnosed, highlighting the need for reliable biomarkers for accurate diagnosis and assessing clinical severity. Tau positron emission tomography (PET) has emerged as a potential tool for detecting 4R tau in vivo. This review summarizes current evidence on tau PET imaging in PSP, focusing on diagnostic differentiation, clinical phenotypes, symptoms, and disease severity. METHODS: A literature search was conducted using PubMed and Google Scholar for studies on tau PET imaging in PSP, including 4R tau pathology and first- and second-generation tau PET tracers. We focused on evidence of regional tracer uptake across diagnoses and PSP phenotypes and associations with clinical symptoms and disease severity. RESULTS: Tau PET demonstrates regional uptake patterns that may differentiate PSP from other tauopathies, clinically similar disorders, and PSP phenotypes. Regional uptake has the potential for characterizing motor and non-motor features, including balance, speech, oculomotor function, cognitive and behavioural changes, sleep disturbances and autonomic dysfunction. However, interpretation remains limited by off-target binding, variable 4R tau affinity, methodological variabilities, and inconsistent correspondence with post-mortem tau burden. CONCLUSION: Tau PET shows potential as a biomarker for diagnosis, clinical characterization, and disease monitoring in PSP, although current limitations restrict its clinical utility. More selective 4R tau tracers, longitudinal studies, PET-to-autopsy validations, further correlations with clinical scales, and standardized PET analysis methods are needed to establish its utility for monitoring disease progression and prognosis.

papers.title: Rehmannioside A alleviates oxidative stress and restores dopaminergic function via the PI3K/Akt pathway in a rotenone-induced Parkinson's disease model.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder; available treatments merely relieve symptoms, and no disease-modifying therapies are currently available. This study sought to explore the neuroprotective effects of Rehmannioside A (Re A) in rotenone-induced PD models and clarify its underlying mechanisms. METHODS: A rotenone-induced PD rat model was established for in vivo experiments, with rats administered graded oral doses of Re A. Motor function was assessed via behavioral tests. Striatal oxidative stress markers and neurotransmitters were detected using biochemical assays and ELISA, respectively. HE staining was applied to observe histopathological alterations in the substantia nigra, and immunohistochemistry was used to visualize tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive neurons. Western blotting was performed to measure TH expression and key proteins of the PI3K/Akt pathway in brain tissue. For in vitro experiments, rotenone-challenged PC12 cells were treated with different concentrations of Re A. Cell viability was tested using CCK-8 assay, oxidative stress indicators were quantified, and protein levels were analyzed by Western blot. The PI3K inhibitor LY294002 was used to validate the reliance of protective effects on the PI3K/Akt pathway. RESULTS: In vivo, Re A significantly rescued weight loss and motor dysfunction, mitigated striatal oxidative stress, and reduced neuronal injury and pyknosis in the substantia nigra, accompanied by an increased number of TH-positive neurons. Re A restored striatal dopamine and its metabolite levels, activated the PI3K/Akt pathway, and upregulated TH protein expression. In vitro, Re A alleviated rotenone-triggered cytotoxicity and oxidative stress, reversed the suppression of PI3K/Akt signaling, and elevated TH expression. papers.title: Singing-based interventions for motor and non-motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease: a systematic review.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by disabling motor and non-motor symptoms. Although pharmacological and rehabilitation interventions improve many motor and non-motor symptoms, persistent impairments commonly remain in domains, including speech, swallowing, gait, and balance, particularly as the disease progresses. For this reason, over the past few years, alternative rehabilitative approaches, such as singing-based interventions, have been used with the aim of addressing symptoms, such as speech impairment, swallowing difficulties, respiratory dysfunction, and mood. OBJECTIVE: We aim to review the evidences on the efficacy of singing interventions on motor and non-motor symptoms in patients with PD. METHODS: A comprehensive literature search of PubMed and Google Scholar was conducted for interventional studies published until December 2025. Results were summarized into five symptom domains: motor function, voice quality, breathing, swallowing, and quality of life. RESULTS: Twenty-six studies involving 1057 patients with PD were included. Singing-based interventions were associated with improvements in motor symptoms, gait, posture, voice quality, respiratory control, and maximum phonation time. Several studies also reported enhanced psychological well-being, social connectedness, and quality of life, with reductions in stress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms. Evidence regarding swallowing outcomes was limited and inconsistent. Considerable heterogeneity in study design, intervention protocols, and outcome measures precluded meta-analysis. CONCLUSION: Singing is a promising adjunct therapy for PD rehabilitation, particularly in domains less responsive to pharmacological treatment. Further high-quality research is needed to establish standardized protocols and assess long-term benefits.

papers.title: Evaluating the Interaction of Alzheimer Biomarker Burden and α-Synuclein Status on Cognitive Trajectories in Parkinson Disease: Methodological Challenges and Power Estimates.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Alzheimer disease (AD) and α-synuclein copathology frequently co-occur in Parkinson disease (PD), but whether their interaction accelerates longitudinal cognitive decline is unknown. OBJECTIVE: To investigate whether the cross-sectional interaction between AD biomarker burden (CSF pTau181/Aβ42 ratio) and α-synuclein seed amplification assay (SAA) status translates to accelerated cognitive decline, and to estimate sample sizes for future co-pathology studies. METHODS: We studied 246 dementia-free PD participants from the Parkinson Precision Medicine Initiative, including genetically enriched subgroups, across seven cognitive domains over 12.9 years. Longitudinal trajectories were modeled using inverse probability of continuation weighted generalized estimating equations with Firth penalization, confirmed by linear mixed-effects and Bayesian joint models. RESULTS: A cross-sectional AD×SAA visuospatial synergy was replicated (P=0.022), but no longitudinal interaction survived false discovery rate correction (all q≥0.180). However, a nominally significant AD×SAA interaction on verbal memory was detected by subject-specific models (P=0.018 to 0.026). Power simulations indicated that 400 to 600 participants under enriched designs, or over 1000 under naturalistic conditions, are required for 80% power. CONCLUSIONS: Cross-sectional biomarker synergies may not predict accelerated longitudinal decline in early PD. Future copathology studies require strict attrition correction, quantitative α-synuclein measures, and targeted enrichment strategies.

papers.title: Coptis chinensis rhizome extract up-regulates ATP13A2 and lysosomal function to reduce neuronal vulnerability in α-synuclein-expressing BE(2)-M17 cells.
papers.journal: Journal of traditional and complementary medicine
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIM: Chinese herbal medicine (CHM) extracts have potential as treatments for Parkinson's disease (PD), but their neuroprotective mechanisms remain unclear. ATPase cation transporter type 13A2 (ATP13A2), a regulator of lysosomal function implicated in α-synuclein pathology, may represent a therapeutic target. This study aimed to identify CHM extracts that enhance ATP13A2 expression and evaluate their neuroprotective effects. papers.title: Mitoxyperilysis and mitochondrial quality control in Parkinson's disease: emerging links to autophagy and neuronal death.
papers.journal: Apoptosis : an international journal on programmed cell death
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second‑most prevalent central‑nervous‑system neurodegenerative disorder, pathologically characterized by progressive midbrain dopaminergic neuron loss and α‑synuclein‑aggregated Lewy bodies. Impaired mitophagy‑autophagy‑lysosomal quality control is a well‑documented upstream feature of PD; however, its characterization as a core causal driver-and how, or whether, mitophagy insufficiency is converted into irreversible dopaminergic neuronal death-remains incompletely resolved and lacks direct human evidence. Mitoxyperilysis is a recently described non‑caspase‑dependent lytic regulated cell‑death pathway. It can be triggered by combined innate‑immune activation and cellular metabolic disturbance, featuring mitochondrial oxidative stress, stable mitochondria‑plasma‑membrane anchoring and focal lipid‑peroxidation‑driven membrane rupture under the primary regulatory influence of the mTORC2-RhoA-cytoskeleton axis, a regulatory role established primarily in non-PD innate-immune and metabolic stress models. Mitophagy deficiency cannot directly initiate mitoxyperilysis but increases neuronal susceptibility by enabling persistent accumulation of ROS‑generating damaged mitochondria. This review summarizes mitoxyperilysis's core features, regulatory cascades and detection approaches, focusing on its bidirectional crosstalk with the mitophagy‑autophagy‑lysosomal system. We discuss how PD‑associated genetic variants, α‑synuclein aggregation and neuroinflammation disrupt mitophagy‑lysosomal homeostasis and may predispose dopaminergic neurons to mitoxyperilysis‑related injury. We overview pre‑clinical therapeutic candidates and potential biomarkers, and consider plausible links to other neurodegenerative diseases, peripheral pathology and aging. papers.title: Epigenetic Gene-Environment Interactions in Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder, characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. While genetic mutations and environmental exposures have both been established as risk factors for PD, emerging evidence has implicated epigenetic modifications as key mediators of gene-environment interactions involved in the pathogenesis of PD. OBJECTIVE: This review aims to systematically characterize the epigenetic regulatory mechanisms that bridge the effects of environmental neurotoxicants and genetic susceptibility in PD, providing a comprehensive synthesis of the current understanding of their functional crosstalk at a molecular level. KEY FINDINGS: Environmental factors drive the pathogenesis of PD through abnormal DNA methylation, dynamic imbalances in histone modification, and non-coding RNA regulatory networks. Here, we detail the mechanisms by which environment-induced epigenetic shifts give rise to the dysregulation of key PD-associated genes, including SNCA CONCLUSION: Systematically exploring epigenetic gene-environment interactions offers detailed insight into the etiology of PD. Given the potential reversibility of specific epigenetic modifications, targeting these pathways may offer a prospective avenue for neuroprotective research. However, further rigorous investigation remains essential to evaluate the clinical viability of these mechanisms as reliable biomarkers or therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Ceruloplasmin in Disorders of the Nervous System.
papers.abstract: Ceruloplasmin (Cp) is a multicopper ferroxidase that links copper handling, iron export, and redox homeostasis. Within the nervous system, these functions are critical because disruption of iron and copper balance can amplify oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and neuronal vulnerability. Although Cp has long been studied as a circulating biomarker, most reports characterize it only by protein concentration, leaving its enzymatic and structural status comparatively unexplored. Here, we synthesize human literature on Cp across major neurological disorders, with attention to studies that assess Cp's ferroxidase activity, oxidation, fragmentation, and copper-binding state alongside its circulating levels. The evidence is by far most extensive in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, which together account for the majority of the reviewed literature: reduced ferroxidase activity, increased Cp oxidation, and altered non-Cp-bound copper are repeatedly linked to disease severity, regional iron accumulation, and biomarker-defined patient subgroups; in several studies, these alterations were independent of total Cp concentration. A smaller but growing body of evidence in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, essential tremor, and the cerebellar ataxias points to a related pattern of Cp-linked iron mishandling contributing to neuronal vulnerability. Preliminary findings from a few small studies in schizophrenia and a single study in obsessive-compulsive disorder further suggest that circulating Cp levels track systemic inflammatory and oxidative states in these conditions. From these investigations, a picture emerges where Cp's functional and structural integrity, rather than its abundance alone, is the more informative correlate of disease-relevant metal dyshomeostasis, most clearly demonstrated in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. papers.title: Gut-Induced Synuclein Propagation: A New Mechanism in Neurodegenerative Disease.
papers.journal: The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
papers.abstract: Gut-induced synuclein propagation has emerged as a potential mechanism linking gastrointestinal disturbances with the development and progression of Parkinson disease and related synucleinopathies. These disorders are characterized by progressive accumulation and spreading of misfolded α-synuclein (α-Syn), leading to selective neuronal dysfunction and degeneration. Although traditionally considered brain-centered diseases, increasing evidence indicates that gastrointestinal abnormalities, peripheral α-Syn pathology, and gut-associated immune alterations may precede neurological manifestations, suggesting that peripheral processes can influence disease evolution. Here, we review clinical, pathological, and experimental evidence supporting the role of intestinal environmental stress, microbial dysregulation, barrier dysfunction, and immune activation in promoting α-Syn misfolding, aggregation, and transmission through interconnected pathways. However, peripheral α-Syn abnormalities alone are unlikely to be sufficient to initiate neurodegeneration, indicating the presence of additional biological constraints. We propose a cumulative-threshold and biological-gates framework in which α-Syn induction, seed formation, propagation efficiency, anatomical connectivity, and neuronal vulnerability collectively determine whether gut-associated pathology progresses into a self-sustaining neurodegenerative cascade. Understanding the determinants that enable gut-induced synuclein propagation may provide new insights into disease heterogeneity and guide biomarker development and mechanism-based therapeutic strategies for synucleinopathies.

Mitochondria-Associated Membranes as a Convergent Hub of Brain Aging: From Neurodegeneration to Cerebral Ischemia.
papers.abstract: Brain aging is the principal risk factor for both neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) and cerebral ischemic disorders, yet the subcellular mechanisms linking these conditions remain incompletely defined. Mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs)-specialized contact sites between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria-sit at the intersection of two well-established hallmarks of aging, mitochondrial dysfunction, and loss of proteostasis, making them an attractive mechanistic node for understanding age-related brain decline. In this review, we propose a MAM-centered framework that unifies neurodegenerative and ischemic brain pathology under the broader paradigm of brain aging. papers.title: Tractography-Based Insights into Neuroplasticity and Clinical Heterogeneity in Parkinson's Disease Subtypes.
papers.journal: The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease shows substantial heterogeneity across motor, cognitive, and non-motor domains, reflecting variable patterns of neurodegeneration and compensation across distributed brain circuits. Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) tractography enables pathway-specific characterization of white-matter alterations and provides a framework for linking clinical subtypes to tract-level patterns that may be obscured by skeleton-based or connectomic averaging. Here, we synthesize white-matter evidence across motor, cognitive, genetic, and prodromal dimensions of PD heterogeneity, using tractography as an organizing framework within a broader dMRI and multimodal context. We review diffusion approaches ranging from diffusion tensor imaging to free-water, neurite, and fixel-based models. We distinguish pathway reconstructions from other diffusion and imaging analyses and consider how complementary approaches inform, but do not uniquely determine, interpretations of degeneration and subtype-specific neuroplasticity. Emerging methods, including harmonization pipelines, radiomic tractometry, and machine learning classifiers, may further improve tract-level sensitivity and reproducibility. Cognitive subtypes illustrate how posterior association and limbic tract degeneration, together with cholinergic and noradrenergic dysfunction, shape clinical progression. Integrating tractography with molecular, genetic, functional, and clinical markers may support subtype-specific biomarkers for risk stratification, prognosis, and targeted neuromodulation or rehabilitation strategies, although longitudinal and external validation is required before routine use.

papers.title: Non-invasive oral magnetoelectric vagus nerve neuromodulation for Parkinson's disease therapy.
papers.abstract: Vagus nerve stimulation has shown promising neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in progressive neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson's disease. However, its invasive nature introduces procedural and device-related risks. Here we introduce a magnetoelectric particulate system for oral delivery and non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation through the gut. The system comprises a magneto-responsive nickel ferrite core and a piezoelectric barium titanate shell, conjugated with capsaicin to specifically target TRPV1 receptors, ensuring effective adherence to the stomach lining after oral administration. Upon magnetic field stimulation, the particles generate electrical pulses that activate vagal afferent fibres, engaging the nucleus tractus solitarius in the brainstem via the gut-brain axis. This activation enhances norepinephrine production in the locus coeruleus and dopamine synthesis in the substantia nigra. Vagal efferent activation triggers the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway, mitigating both neuroinflammation and systemic inflammation. This non-invasive approach demonstrates potential for alleviating motor symptoms and non-motor anxiety in Parkinson's disease, offering valuable insights into its mechanisms and clinical applications.

papers.title: Clinical Trajectory of Late-Onset Delusional Disorder Toward Evolving Dementia With Lewy Bodies.
papers.journal: Psychogeriatrics : the official journal of the Japanese Psychogeriatric Society
papers.abstract: Recent clinical observations indicate that late-onset psychosis can precede the onset of dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). However, its longitudinal clinical trajectory remains poorly understood. Delusional disorder (DD) in older adults is relatively uncommon and poor insight frequently leads to refusal of psychiatric care, limiting available data despite its long-standing diagnostic recognition. This article focuses on late-onset DD in relation to subsequent development of DLB. We revisited our previously reported cases in which delusions were the initial manifestation of Lewy body disease (LBD) and aimed to identify the shared clinical features to help delineate more homogeneous subgroups within the heterogeneous spectrum of late-onset psychosis. These cases with late-onset DD revealed a recurring phenotype characterised by onset in the 50s and 60s, reluctance to seek psychiatric care, eventual hospitalisation, poor antipsychotic tolerance and delayed emergence of dementia accompanied by core features of DLB. Clinicopathological examination of four cases raises the hypothesis that persistent delusions may emerge in the presence of relatively restricted Lewy pathology, preceding the development of widespread cortical involvement and overt dementia. Relative preservation of neuronal populations in the substantia nigra may account for the absence of parkinsonism during the early phases dominated by isolated delusions. Despite long-standing delusions beginning in the 50s and 60s, a common age range for DLB onset (mid-70s and older) was observed, indicating an exceptionally prolonged prodromal period. These findings suggest that late-onset DD associated with LBD may follow a clinical trajectory distinct from that of mild cognitive impairment with Lewy bodies (MCI-LB), the most common clinical phenotype of prodromal DLB. papers.title: Estimating bone marrow adiposity from head MRI and identifying its genetic architecture.
papers.abstract: Bone marrow (BM) adiposity changes radically through the lifespan, but this phenomenon is poorly characterized and understood in humans. Large datasets of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans of the head have been collected to study the human brain, but also contain unexploited information about other organs. We developed an artificial neural network that localizes calvarial BM in T1-weighted MRI head scans, enabling us to study its composition in several large MRI datasets, and to model sex-dimorphic age trajectories, including the effect of menopause. We revealed high heritability in single-nucleotide polymorphism and twin data, and identified 41 genetic loci significantly associated with the trait, including six sex-specific loci. Integrating mapped genes with existing BM single-cell RNA-sequencing data revealed patterns of adipogenic lineage differentiation and lipid loading. Finally, we identified significant genetic correlations with several human traits, including cognitive ability and Parkinson's disease, which is intriguing in light of the recently discovered channels that link calvarial BM to the meninges.
